meta.location: The land of Zarahemla; the hill Amnihu; the valley of Gideon; the river Sidon

world_behind.title: The system's first contested use, five years in
world_behind.text: Mosiah 29 built a government on the voice of the people and the record has run four quiet years on it. This is the first time the instrument is pointed at something a large faction badly wants, and the losing side refuses the result two verses after it is announced.

world_behind.title: The failure that arrives is not the one that was predicted
world_behind.text: Mosiah warned that a majority might choose iniquity and said what would follow. Here the majority chooses correctly. What breaks is the minority's willingness to be bound, which nobody had thought to name.

world_behind.title: Amlici is introduced as Nehor's heir in the opening sentence
world_behind.text: Before his ambition is mentioned he is placed "after the order of the man that slew Gideon by the sword, who was executed according to the law." The chapter opens by reminding the reader that this order has already killed one man and lost one.

world_behind.title: A second title, unannounced
world_behind.text: Verse 16 calls Alma "the chief judge and the governor of the people of Nephi." Mosiah 29 had created a chief judge and said nothing about a governor, and the word has not been used before in this record. The office picks up its military name the first time it has to lead an army.

world_behind.title: A faction becomes a people by taking a name
world_behind.text: Verse 11 has the followers of Amlici distinguished by his name and called Amlicites, and the remainder called Nephites. A vote produced two parties; a name produces two nations, and the war follows the naming rather than the ballot.

world_behind.title: The map of the next forty chapters is drawn here
world_behind.text: The river Sidon, the hill Amnihu, the land of Minon, the valley of Gideon and the wilderness of Hermounts all enter the record in this chapter. Sidon goes on to appear thirty-seven times; three of the others are never mentioned again.

world_behind.title: Precise totals, down to the single soul
world_behind.text: Verse 19 gives exact figures for both sides. Zeniff had done that once in his own first-person account of a much smaller war; this is the first time the abridgment itself puts numbers on a battle.

words.text: Skilled, knowing. The word means competence, with the older neutral sense still attached. The verse uses it twice over: a very cunning man, and a wise man as to the wisdom of the world. That second phrase has appeared once before in the record, describing Lamanites who had learned to trade and grow great. The word marks ability that has been aimed somewhere.

Causing wonder, astonishing, in the older sense that has nothing pleasant in it. The people held "much dispute and wonderful contentions one with another" while deciding how to vote. The pairing is unique in scripture and the word appears only four times in this record. What it registers is the size of the argument, not its quality.

As a verb: to bring under. Amlici's first command as king is that his people take up arms against their brethren, "that he might subject them to him." The record uses the verb three times, and every one of them belongs to somebody trying to own a population rather than govern one.

A curved sword. Enos put the word in the record first, listing what the Lamanites were skilled with: the bow, the cimeter, and the ax. By this verse the Nephites are carrying them too, in a weapons list that runs to eleven items.
The hill east of Sidon where the Amlicites made their stand. The name is unique in scripture. It is given, used once, and never written again. The record names the ground and then drops it.

Trained by practice, worked at. Alma is "being exercised with much faith" in the middle of a sword fight. The only other place scripture joins the verb to that preposition is Peter's description of a heart exercised with covetous practices. Both are about what long habit has made a person good at.

The wilderness west and north where the survivors scattered. The name is unique in scripture and the verse exists to say what is in it: wild and ravenous beasts. The place is named so that the next verse can report what happened to the wounded.

phrases.term: A wise man as to the wisdom of the world
phrases.text: A compliment with a fence around it. The qualifier does all the work. He is wise in the way the world measures wisdom, and the sentence declines to say anything further. The record has used the phrase once before, of Lamanites growing rich by trade.

phrases.term: After the order of the man that slew Gideon by the sword
phrases.text: Nehor is not named, he is described by his crime. A movement is identified by the worst thing its founder did, and the same sentence adds that he was executed according to the law. The reader is told what this order costs before being told what it wants.

phrases.term: Every man according to his mind
phrases.text: The description of a free vote, and the clause is unique in scripture. Each person assembles by his own judgment, into separate bodies, for or against. The record has no word for a ballot, so it describes one by saying what each man was doing with his mind.

phrases.term: To cast in their voices concerning the matter
phrases.text: The mechanism, in the record's own words. The phrase appears twice in scripture: once when the people first chose judges under Mosiah's reform, and once here. Both are the same act; only the second one has a losing side that refuses to accept it.

phrases.term: The voice of the people came against Amlici
phrases.text: The result, with no margin reported and no count. Twenty-three words settle the only question the chapter poses, and this is the one place where the new constitution actually functions. What follows is thirty-one verses about people who will not live with it.

phrases.term: The remainder were called Nephites, or the people of God
phrases.text: The majority has to be renamed too. Before this verse they were simply the people; a faction leaving forces everyone left behind into a category, and the record supplies two names for them in the same breath. Secession changes the identity of the side that stayed.

phrases.term: Spare my life, that I may be an instrument in thy hands
phrases.text: A prayer offered mid-duel, and it asks for usefulness. "Instrument in the hands of God" is what the record called Gideon two chapters back, right before Nehor killed him, so the phrase has already been shown not to guarantee survival.

phrases.term: He cleared the ground, or rather the bank
phrases.text: The narrator correcting himself again. He did the same thing nineteen verses into the previous chapter, at Nehor's execution, and "or rather" turns up eleven times across this record. It is the habit of a man working from sources and unwilling to let a first phrasing stand when a more exact one occurs to him. Here he does it in the middle of describing bodies thrown into a river.

verses.label: v. 1–4
verses.title: A candidate, and what the law required of him
verses.text: Amlici is cunning, worldly-wise, and of Nehor's order. His following grows large enough to be called powerful, and they set out to make him king. The church is alarmed, and the reason given is procedural: such things must be established by the voice of the people. The fear stated in verse 4 is that a lawful vote could deliver a man who would destroy the church lawfully.

verses.label: v. 5–9
verses.title: The vote, and what happened after it
verses.text: Assembly throughout the land, separate bodies, much dispute, voices cast and laid before the judges. The voice comes against Amlici. Joy on one side, anger stirred on the other, and then his supporters gather by themselves and crown him. The whole procedure is honored and then discarded inside five verses.

verses.label: v. 10–14
verses.title: Two names, and two armies
verses.text: His first command as king is to take up arms against their brethren, and the stated purpose is subjection. The record supplies the names, Amlicites and Nephites, and then two matching inventories: weapons on both sides, captains and higher captains on one, rulers and leaders on the other.

verses.label: v. 15–20
verses.title: The battle, the count, and a valley
verses.text: They meet on the hill Amnihu east of Sidon. Alma goes at the head of his armies, chief judge and governor both. The Nephites fall until the Lord strengthens their hand; then the pursuit, and the numbers: twelve thousand five hundred thirty-two and six thousand five hundred sixty-two. That night they camp in the valley of Gideon.

verses.label: v. 21–27
verses.title: Spies, and a second enemy
verses.text: Four men are sent and all four are named (Zeram, Amnor, Manti, Limher), though none of them appears again. They come back astonished: the Amlicites have joined a Lamanite host in the land of Minon, and Nephite families are fleeing toward Zarahemla ahead of them. The chapter's threat doubles between two verses.

verses.label: v. 28–34
verses.title: The duel at the river
verses.text: The Nephites cross Sidon and are met. They are strengthened, the record says, because they had prayed mightily. Then Alma and Amlici fight face to face; Alma prays in the middle of it and kills him. He fights the Lamanite king, who flees and sends his guards. The passage ends with bodies thrown into the water to clear the bank.

verses.label: v. 35–38
verses.title: The pursuit, and what the wilderness did
verses.text: The enemy flees west and north beyond the borders, pursued and slain, into a wilderness infested with wild and ravenous beasts. The last verse follows the wounded there: dead of their wounds, devoured by beasts and vultures, bones found and heaped on the ground. The chapter ends on what was left rather than on who won.

chapter.title: The election works, and that is exactly the problem
chapter.text: Nothing in the procedure fails. The country assembles, disputes, votes, and the count is delivered to the judges. The constitution holds up perfectly and produces a civil war anyway, because a system that settles questions only binds people who agreed in advance to be settled.

chapter.title: Amlici takes by force precisely what the vote refused him
chapter.text: He wanted to be king; the voice said no; his faction crowned him regardless. The record lays the sequence out without editorial: stir up to anger, gather together, consecrate, command them to take up arms. The flatness of the telling is what makes it legible.

chapter.title: A religious order has become a political party
chapter.text: Nehor preached a labor policy and killed a man over it. Five years later his order fields a candidate, contests a national vote, raises an army, and allies with a foreign power. The chapter shows a heresy completing its journey into a faction.

chapter.title: The chapter does more naming than any before it
chapter.text: Amlicites and Nephites in verse 11; the valley of Gideon in verse 20; four spies named in verse 22 who never reappear; Amnihu, Minon, Sidon and Hermounts. The record is laying down the vocabulary the next forty chapters will need, and it does it in the middle of a battle.

chapter.title: The chief judge fights in the line
chapter.text: Alma is high priest, chief judge, and here also governor and a combatant in single combat. The offices Mosiah 29 separated from the crown are all sitting on one man, and that man is swinging a sword at the head of an army. The record notes it and does not comment.

chapter.title: The prayer asks for usefulness
chapter.text: Alma does not ask to win; he asks to live in order to be an instrument in God's hands to save and preserve his people. The record had used that same description of Gideon two chapters earlier, immediately before Gideon was cut down. The phrase carries no promise about how the fight ends.

chapter.title: The record counts the dead once and then gives up
chapter.text: Verse 19 is precise to the single soul on both sides. Alma 3:1 reports that the slain were not numbered because of the greatness of their number. Between those two sentences the war stops being something that can be added up.

chapter.title: Role in the book
chapter.text: This is the first secession in Nephite history, and the template for every one that follows: a man who wants to be king, a faction that will not accept a vote, a name taken to mark the split, and an alliance with the Lamanites. The Amalekites, the king-men, and Amalickiah all run this play again.

applications.title: Notice what a compliment is fenced off from
applications.text: He was wise as to the wisdom of the world. The qualifier is the whole judgment, and it is delivered without insult. Praising accurately often means naming the category the ability belongs to.

applications.title: Decide in advance that you will lose well
applications.text: The vote was fair, publicly conducted, and reported. What broke was the losers' willingness to be bound by it. Any agreement you enter is only worth what you will do the first time it goes against you.

applications.title: Watch for the moment a disagreement acquires a name
applications.text: Amlicites and Nephites appear in the same sentence, and the fighting starts after that. Naming a side hardens it; it is worth knowing when you are doing it.

applications.title: Pray to be useful
applications.text: Alma asks for his life, and gives the reason in the same breath: that he might be an instrument to save and preserve the people. The request has a purpose attached, which is what makes it something other than fear.

applications.title: Do the ordinary thing before the crisis arrives
applications.text: After the victory Alma sends spies, wanting to know their plans and their plots. The chapter's most useful decision is a piece of routine caution taken while everyone else was celebrating.

applications.title: Bury your own dead and name the ground
applications.text: The valley is called after Gideon, and the sentence naming it also names who killed him. Places that carry what happened in them do a kind of remembering that no one has to keep doing on purpose.

applications.title: Expect the ending to be about the wounded
applications.text: The chapter does not close on the victory; it follows the injured into Hermounts and stops at their bones. Whatever a conflict was about, this is what it produces, and the record insists on the last look.

questions.text: What ability of mine is worldly-wise and pointed at nothing worth having?
When a decision went against me, what did I do in the next two days?
What ceremony have I staged to make something legitimate that a fair process refused?
Which name do I wear that makes someone else automatically the other side?
If my life were spared this year, what would I say it was for?
Whose wounds am I not following far enough to see?
